title: MiFID II
text: In the European Union, the rulebook for trading firms is MiFID II. It has applied since 3 January 2018. It treats an algorithm as something a firm must test, limit and be able to stop.

title: Why it matters
text: Article 17 of the directive is the core for trading firms. A firm that trades algorithmically must tell its regulator, and have effective systems and risk controls. The engineering detail sits in RTS 6, Delegated Regulation 2017/589. And high-frequency traders carry extra duties, so the rules define them with numbers.

title: Who counts as HFT
text: A high-frequency technique has three parts. Infrastructure built to cut latency, such as co-location or proximity hosting. Orders decided by the system, with no human in each decision. And a high message rate: on average, at least 2 messages per second in any one instrument on a venue, or 4 per second across all instruments there. Firms that meet the test must keep a record of every order, and hold it for five years.

title: RTS 6 controls
text: RTS 6 turns Article 17 into a checklist. Before an algorithm goes live, it must be tested so it does not behave in an unintended manner. Every order passes pre-trade controls: price collars, maximum order value, maximum order volume, and message limits. A kill function must cancel all unexecuted orders at once, on every venue. Real-time alerts must fire within five seconds of the event. After trading, the firm reconciles its logs with its brokers' and venues' records. And once a year, it signs off a self-assessment.

title: Clock sync
text: Every reportable event needs a timestamp traceable to UTC. Under RTS 25, an HFT firm's clocks had to stay within 100 microseconds of UTC, stamped to the microsecond. Other algorithmic trading got one millisecond. Since 2 March 2026, those rules live in a new MiFIR standard, Regulation 2025/1155. It keeps the 100 microsecond limit for HFT, but asks for timestamps to a tenth of a microsecond.

title: In the lab
text: The lab's pre-trade risk reads like an RTS 6 checklist. A 5 percent price collar around the mid. A maximum order of 1,000 shares and $100,000 notional. A message limit of 2,000 orders a second, as a token bucket. A kill switch that blocks everything, while cancels always pass. And after the day, the drop copy lets the firm reconcile its fills against the exchange's record.

title: Takeaway
text: So what do pros do? They treat RTS 6 as an engineering spec, not paperwork. They test every algorithm change before it trades. They rehearse the kill switch, and log which algorithm sent each order. And they keep clocks traceable to UTC, with the evidence. This is education, not legal advice.
